newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian woman seeks right to die under law.
newsitem.headline: Australian woman seeks right to die under law.

text.p: An Australian woman with terminal cancer begged on Thursday for a doctor to sign medical documents allowing her to be the second person to die using the world's only voluntary euthanasia law before it is overturned.
Janet Mills, 52, who has only weeks to live, said she was seeking the third and final doctor's signature necessary under the law to end her life.
"I know I have only a few weeks left to live and I am asking, begging really, for this signature," Mills told a news conference in Darwin in the outback Northern Territory.
"This will then allow me the right to end this ordeal and to die with my family present, in an open, dignified and humane manner," Mills said.

Mills has a rare form of skin cancer called mycosis fungoides which sees the skin disintegrate. In 1995 British comic actor Paul Eddington, star of the BBC's "Yes, Minister" series, died from the same cancer.

The world's first euthanasia law came into effect in July in the Northern Territory. In September, Australian cancer patient Bob Dent, 66, became the first and only person to use the law through a computer-delivered lethal injection.
Mills gave her news conference at Dent's Darwin home.

On Tuesday the Australian parliament's lower house, the House of Representatives, voted to overturn the voluntary euthanasia law. The anti-euthanasia bill will go before the upper house Senate next year for final approval.

Opinion polls show around 75 percent of Australians support voluntary euthanasia. Euthanasia is only legal in the Northern Territory, although many doctors concede that it is carried out unofficially in the rest of the country.
Mills, who is from South Australia state, travelled to Darwin three months ago to use the law, but has so far found it impossible to gain the necessary three medical signatures.

Under the law a terminally-ill person needs the signatures of a doctor, a psychiatrist and a Northern Territory resident specialist. But doctors have been warned they may face criminal charges if they assist a death and the law is overturned.
Dr Philip Nitschke, dubbed "Doctor Death" by anti-euthanasia groups for assisting the first legal mercy killing, has signed Mills' documents, along with a psychiatrist.
"What we need is a Territory-resident cancer specialist to provide that last elusive signature," Nitschke told Reuters by telephone from Darwin.
"The minute she gets that she wants to start the seven-day cooling-off period and then go ahead and use the law as fast as she can," he said.
But Nitschke, who accompanied Mills at the news conference, said Mills may die before she can use the euthanasia law.
"You have to be pessimistic...but this is her last chance," Nitschke said. "She has made a very public appeal...but there is probably only a slim hope."
In July, cancer-stricken taxi driver Max Bell, 66, failed to gain the three signatures and later died.
Nitschke said there were five people, including Mills, currently seeking to use the voluntary euthanasia law.
